analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from denying workers federally required health coverage, including birth control.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote; it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court ruled in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby that some for-profit employers could refuse to cover contraception in their health plans on religious grounds, this bill would have overridden that result. It says that whenever an employer offers a health plan, it must cover every item or service federal law requires — including contraception — and that this rule applies even though the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 says otherwise. It also lets federal agencies adjust the rules for religious employers. The bill was referred to three House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — mostly women — whose employers object on religious grounds to covering contraception. Before the bill, employees at objecting closely held corporations could lose no-cost contraceptive coverage that the Affordable Care Act otherwise guaranteed; the bill would have restored that guarantee for all federally required benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any employer that offers a group health plan to cover every specific item or service required under federal law or regulation, rather than being able to carve coverage out [S2][S3].

Applies notwithstanding the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, directly overriding the effect of the Supreme Court's 2014 Hobby Lobby decisions, which allowed some for-profit corporations to exclude contraceptive coverage [S2][S3].
Restores no-cost contraceptive coverage the bill's findings say had reached 47 million women and saved them $483 million in out-of-pocket costs for oral contraceptives in 2013 alone [S3].
Enforces the requirement through the same mechanisms used for other group health plan rules, with penalties on plan sponsors, plans, and insurers that fail to comply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with religious objections lose the ability to exclude contraceptive coverage from plans they sponsor. Health plans and insurers must provide the required coverage; any added plan costs are shared among employers, premiums, and the broader risk pool. Religious employers would remain subject to a modified exemption left to agency regulations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Objecting employers and their health plans

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, a law Congress itself passed in 1993 to protect religious exercise — a genuine conflict for those who see closely held employers' objections as a matter of conscience, and the Supreme Court had just ruled for those employers [S3].

Mandated coverage without cost-sharing adds covered services to plans; the bill's own findings argue this is offset because plans without contraceptive coverage cost employers 15 to 17 percent more in pregnancy and related costs, but the mandate does constrain how plans are designed [S3].

The bill leaves the scope of the religious-employer exemption to future regulation by three departments, so the exact boundary between religious liberty and coverage would have been settled by administrative rulemaking rather than the statute [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of women whose contraceptive coverage was at stake after the Hobby Lobby ruling, the benefit is direct and immediate: no-cost coverage restored regardless of the employer's views. The cost falls narrowly on objecting employers and modestly on plan costs, and the bill's findings argue that covering contraception reduces overall employer costs. The main honest objection is the override of a religious-freedom statute — a real constitutional-values tradeoff, but one that resolves in favor of the employee rather than the employer.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and two subcommittees and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on July 9, 2014, days after the Supreme Court's Hobby Lobby decisions, with 162 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred to three committees — Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means — splitting it among committees with overlapping jurisdiction [S5].
It was referred to subcommittees on July 11, 2014 and again on November 17, 2014, but no committee or subcommittee took it up further [S5].
No vote was ever scheduled in the House, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with religious objections kept the right, affirmed by the Supreme Court, to exclude contraceptive coverage from their employees' plans; the 47 million women the bill cited as beneficiaries of no-cost coverage remained exposed to employer carve-outs.

sides.party_line_note: All 163 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with a Republican House majority the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Employers with religious objections to contraception coverage
industries.note: The bill would have stripped these employers — closely held for-profit corporations, after Hobby Lobby — of the ability to exclude contraceptive coverage from employee plans. The bill's findings note dozens of lawsuits by employers seeking that carve-out [S3].

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: Plans and insurers would have had to provide all federally required coverage regardless of the sponsoring employer's objection, an added obligation for the affected slice of the market. Insurers otherwise sell the mandated coverage; the mandate is the vehicle for the benefit to employees.

The bill directs federal agencies to adjust the contraceptive-coverage rules for religious employers consistent with its purposes, leaving church-plan accommodations largely in place while ending the carve-out for for-profit firms [S2][S3].
